The 30 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes determined in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them, the number of groups being set at 3. Where a cluster contains only one product, the method of preparation determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.
2088: Of the 3 clusters, 2 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another to a greater extent than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) applied Ward's method comparably in rice and drew upon the cluster means to select genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to generate useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) advanced the same point from the product side, namely that different traditional preparations require genuinely different raw material.

Each was grown and prepared identically for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. The principal finding is therefore unambiguous: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production is of markedly less consequence. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally retain its position in the next.

2103: This experiment was undertaken to examine the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal together with one non-aromatic control. The experiment was laid out in a two-factor completely randomised design with three replications and was repeated in two years. Factor A was variety, namely Gobindabhog (G), Radhunipagal (R), Kalojira (K) and the non-aromatic control Dudeshwar (D); Factor B was product, namely plain idli (I), idli fortified with carrot extract (CI) and idli fortified with beet extract (BI). This yielded twelve treatment combinations, designated DBI, DCI, DI, GBI, GCI, GI, KBI, KCI, KI, RBI, RCI and RI. The results are presented and discussed below.
2105: The two years of data were combined only after the error variances had been tested by the Bartlett chi-square test (Gomez and Gomez, 1984). The test proved non-significant for most characters, demonstrating that the error variances of the two years were comparable and that the data could legitimately be pooled. It was significant only for manganese, ash, PGI and springiness; for these four characters an Aitken transformation was applied prior to the analysis of variance, and the transformed means were used for testing significance (Panse and Sukhatme, 1985).
2106: The experiment was precise. The coefficient of variation fell below 3% for most characters and was lowest for calcium (0.20%), total phenol and total antioxidant activity (0.34% each). Higher values were recorded for fat (15.91%), resilience (11.71%), copper (9.65%) and anthocyanin (9.63%); such values are to be expected for constituents present in small quantities and determined after extraction (Das and Giri, 1986).
2107: The variety × product interaction was highly significant for most of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters, indicating that the four varieties did not respond uniformly to fortification. The interaction was non-significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability.
2108: In the tables that follow, the values for the two years and the pooled value of the twelve treatment combinations are given as mean plus or minus standard deviation. The annual values are means of three replications and the pooled values means of six observations. The standard error of the mean, the critical difference at the 5% level and the coefficient of variation are given beneath each table. Pooled means followed by the same letter do not differ significantly at the 5% level. Each table is followed by a figure presenting the pooled means, in which the vertical bars denote the standard error of the mean and the letters above the bars the groupings at the 5% level.
2110: Amylose determines the cooking and eating quality of rice products, since it governs the extent of starch retrogradation on cooling and therefore the firmness or stickiness of the product (Juliano, 1992; Tester et al., 2004). Amylose ranged from 16.75% in DI to 9.78% in RBI (Table 4.99), DI being at par with KI (16.25%). All twelve combinations fall within the low-amylose group of Juliano (1992), which accounts for the soft, moist texture of idli prepared from these small-grained landraces (Singh et al., 2000). Within each variety, amylose declined from the plain product to the carrot-fortified and thence to the beet-fortified product; the magnitude of this decline differed between varieties, which is why the interaction proved significant.
2111: Starch exhibited the same pattern, ranging from 51.66% in DI to 24.05% in GBI (Table 4.100), and total carbohydrate from 60.21% in DI to 40.91% in KBI (Table 4.101). Two mechanisms account for the decline in the fortified treatments. First, the vegetable extract dilutes the rice and black gram base (Sharma et al., 2012; Chhikara et al., 2019). Second, the amylolytic microflora of the batter degrades a proportion of the starch during fermentation (Steinkraus, 1996; Nout, 2009). The non-aromatic control returned higher starch and carbohydrate than the aromatic landraces, which corroborates Verma and Srivastav (2017).
2112: Total soluble sugar behaved inversely, rising from 0.53% in RI to 3.83% in RBI (Table 4.102). Beetroot is rich in free sugars (Singh and Hathan, 2014), and the amylases of the fermenting microflora liberate further reducing sugars from the rice starch (Blandino et al., 2003).
2113: Resistant starch is the fraction escaping digestion in the small intestine and undergoing fermentation in the colon (Englyst et al., 1992; Sajilata et al., 2006). It ranged from 1.97% in DCI to 1.02% in KBI (Table 4.103), and non-resistant starch from 50.78% in DI to 23.57% in GBI (Table 4.104). The carrot-fortified treatments returned the highest resistant starch, attributable to the dietary fibre contributed by carrot and to the retrogradation of amylose as the steamed product cools, which generates the RS3 fraction (Sajilata et al., 2006).
2114: The predicted glycaemic index, determined by the in vitro method of Goñi et al. (1997), ranged from 58.46 in RCI to 75.08 in KBI (Table 4.105). Treatments of higher resistant starch returned a lower glycaemic index, which confirms the finding of Frei et al. (2003) that the resistant fraction, rather than total starch, governs the glycaemic response of rice foods. Carrot fortification is therefore preferable to beet fortification where a low-glycaemic product is required, since carrot fibre retards enzyme access to the starch granule (Sharma et al., 2012).
2115: Total soluble protein, estimated by the method of Lowry et al. (1951), ranged from 2.71% in KBI to 1.05% in DI (Table 4.106), and total protein from 13.44% in KI to 10.92% in DCI (Table 4.107). The idli was richer in protein than milled rice for two reasons: the black gram in the batter supplies lysine-rich protein compensating for the lysine-poor protein of rice (Reddy et al., 1981; Ufaz and Galili, 2008), and fermentation augments protein through microbial growth and proteolysis (Chavan and Kadam, 1989; Ghosh and Chattopadhyay, 2011). The aromatic landraces returned more protein than the control, and Radhunipagal combined high protein with low amylose, which accords with the negative relation between grain protein and amylose reported by Chattopadhyay et al. (2018).
